projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert S. Storms was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the World War II veteran Robert S. Storms. Mr. Storms served in the U.S. Army in the European Theater, and his highest rank was corporal. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Storms's home in Avon Lake, Ohio, on February 9th, 2004. Robert was 81 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: In -- I was living in Niles, Michigan.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: And we were -- I went to -- at that time, war -- let's see. War had been declared in '40. I think -- well, I was at Michigan State at the time that war was declared. My brother and I were --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have -- before we get to that, do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yes. I remember I was -- my brother and I were studying in the dorm. It was Wells Hall. It's not there anymore. And it was -- we were studying, and we both said, "My gosh. They're at war. Do you think we're -- do you think we'll have to go?" You know, the idea -- I mean, we didn't know what was going -- we were in the ROTC. We were in calvary ROTC in college. And so they -- the school stepped up all of that. So, I mean, you really got into the training then. I mean, they were -- they were for ROTC in those days, I mean, because that was a land-grant college, and that was -- it was required. So we took it, and I -- we liked horses, so we thought, hey, this is a good thing to get into. And so at that time, that's what we -- we continued on. And we -- we enlisted then to -- we went to the draft board and told them, "We're ready to go." And they said, well, we could -- at that time, you could finish out your year, so as long as they knew you were in -- we wanted to get into the calvary, so that's why -- we thought, well, this is something we know about. So we did, and that's -- and so we enlisted and then we went in.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And just so we know, this is your twin brother. His name is Ed --

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah. Is Ed Storms, yeah. And he lives in 3811 Kay Drive in Stow, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. So when did you enlist then actually? In '42?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: No. It was in '40 -- last part of '41, but we didn't go in till '42 --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Till the end of '41 --

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: -- I mean -- well, I mean, it was the last -- yeah, on -- yeah, then we went in then, and so that's -- so...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where did you train then?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Oh, we went down to -- well, the first -- first days we were at Fort Custer at -- in Kalamazoo. And then we went down to -- you know, till they weed everybody out and tell them, you know, where -- whatever outfit you're going. So then we went down to Texas. No, no. Oh, just hold it a minute. I'm trying to think. No. This is -- you shouldn't do this to me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't --

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: It's been too -- it's been too long.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't need specific information.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Well, it was -- it was for the calvary in -- down in Texas. And we joined the outfit down there, and that's where we got our basic training.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So then you joined -- at that point, did you join the 14th Calvary?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: No, no. That one -- we were just in calvary at that time. I mean, it was a horse calvary outfit in Fort Riley. Fort Riley, Kansas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Now we got it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: I remembered it after we talked about it. Yeah. So that's where we got our basic training in horse calvary down there. And we were there for, I don't know, whatever the amount of time. I forget now how long you're supposed to be. But then the war became more -- well, started to heat up more so -- and we knew the only way the horse calvary was going to go would be to Japan, and they needed people in Europe at the time. So they put us in pioneering demolition, which we learned about the bombs and, you know, laying the material like that on bridges and stuff. And so then we were shipped out to Oregon, which was the 18th Calvary Reconnaissance Squadron, and we were in the 14th Calvary Group, Troop B. So that's where we -- that's where we ended up and did all our training.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any stories from your training that come to mind? Anything exciting or unusual?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Well, the -- not really, except -- no, there -- it was pretty -- it was pretty basic. Well, we did -- we all -- we were in a, say, closed cadre outfit. I mean, the men that were there were old Army. We were -- all the guys that were -- came in then were the new recruits, I mean. And so advancement was pretty -- I mean, everybody had to learn everybody's job. I mean, we had to know what the tankers did, what -- and they had to know what we did, you know, all the pioneering demolition. We all had to know radio, we all had -- the map stuff, you know, and the gun, all the gun. We had to know everybody's stuff so if somebody went down, the next guy could do it. And it didn't make any difference who was -- what the rank was, I mean, which was kind of an interesting part for that. Because it was small. It was a specialized little unit and -- which we enjoyed that. And the -- and so that's -- that was pretty much it then. We did mostly your gun work and, you know, radio stuff and all that business like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you go through the whole training then with your brother then? Was he --

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: No. Well, he was in Troop C, and I was in Troop B. And I -- his troop commander said I could come over to his place, but he couldn't come over to mine. I mean, they didn't want both of us together. I mean, that was just a little bit -- you know, after the Sullivan guys, you know, where the whole family -- and so they -- neither one of us could get together. But we were within where we could see each other every now and then, on -- on weekends or something like that if we wanted -- if we wanted to get together, you know, you could do that. And so it was -- it made a nice part of it for family because -- but then you made your own friends, and he had his guys with Troop C and I had with Troop B. But now, after this is all over, when we go to a reunion, they're all mixed together and everybody knows, you know, everybody, and it's not -- and half of them didn't know which one of us was which anyhow when we were there so -- and even now, half of his guys call me Ed, and I'm, "Wrong, Bill. I'm Bob." So -- so, but, you know, they -- they do it. And, you know, when you're in the Army, you begin to look more and more alike. Except now we're a lot older, wrinkler, and look like old prunes. But outside of that, we're the same. But -- so then we went overseas and -- is that --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you still training with horses then at the calvary or --

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: No, no, no. Then, we were completely mechanized then. So all of us had your Jeeps, your armored cars, and any kind of -- and some tanks, but -- and all of them had guns, gun mounts on your -- on your little Jeeps and all that. So you had 30-calibers or -- and it's -- we were pretty well for fire power -- for a little group, you had a lot of fire power, but not -- but for what we did. I mean, the idea was that you go ahead, find out where the enemy is, report back, and then you would have your -- you'd have your rest period. I mean, you were attached to armies this way. I mean, it wasn't like if the Second Army needed recon for something and you were, say, available, you -- you were -- that's where you went. Just before the Bulge, the Second Army needed us, so we were with them. It was near the Christmas area. Then we went up into the Ardennes for a while, just to park ourselves for -- I mean, it was just going to be just for a couple weeks, and then -- but we were stretched so thin, you -- it was -- it was impossible to -- to cover. But that was supposed to -- at that time, that area was not supposed to be a vulnerable part, where nothing was going to come through. But, you know, in our outfit, we could -- I could see the Germans. We could see the Germans. They were in their bunkers over there. I could -- I could see them, and I'd get our guys out. I'd say, "Okay." I was the mortar corporal then. I'd -- "Let's go and let's have a little practice." They'd be hanging up their laundry, and I'd say, "Okay. Let's pump about five rounds." "Poom, poom." And we'd pump them over there, and we'd pack up now, and we'd go back in, and then they'd -- you could see them over there, and then they -- so they'd send a few rounds back, but they didn't know quite where -- where it was. And at night, we would have our outposts out there, and they would -- and this was in the wintertime. It started to snow and get bad. And you could see them come through. They'd come crawling through, but you never shot at them. And there was a little town right behind us. And the next day, you'd find all these men. They were in civilian clothes, you know. They -- new -- new men, so you knew they were the soldiers. And they were looking for where the outposts were all along here, so we knew something was coming along. And we would send this back to headquarters. Nobody took any -- and we could hear their tanks winding up. And you know when they start winding up those babies that something is going to happen. And, oh, no. This was supposed to not be a place of any kind of attack. Well, something else. And so we went -- and we even sent men out at night and picked up prisoners, and we'd get guys from the Swiss Navy. And so you knew they were cannon -- the cannon fodder, the guys that were going to be put in the front line, and then they changed the epaulets on their shoulders, so that meant usually that a -- some kind of an attack was coming. When they -- when they -- why, I don't know, but this is just seemingly what happened. And so it was -- it was quite -- we knew something was going to happen. And -- and then the 106th moved in up on our right flank, and they were just 18 days out of the states. And we would try to get radio communications. Well, they didn't want any of that because they were -- I mean, supposedly this was war, you know, and they didn't want anybody to know whatever -- whatever it was, they wouldn't give us radio communications. We would even send guys up there, and they wouldn't -- they didn't want to anything about it, anything to do with anybody else. And on their outposts, when these guys would come through, they -- these guys would shoot rounds until they were circling out on -- you know, really, and they found out how far all their guns would traverse and the whole thing. And so on the day of the Bulge, when this started, they were all gone. They knew just how to get -- how far they could go, you know, how far their guns would shoot. You know, they weren't matched, you know, because they were new. And so a good share of the 106th was really wiped out. I met some of them later, and they said, "Jeez, they even got the" -- not priests, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The chaplains?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: The chaplains. They were intact. They got everybody, so -- which was a sad happening for young groups. But they were -- you know, they were young, and they -- and they didn't -- and we had been there for a while, so that -- so that then -- you know, so you were kind of -- you knew what was happening, and so you let them do it. I made drawings of that, you know, of the -- you know, you could see them in the white snow, but you could see their breath coming out. And you'd say -- you'd radio back, "Well, there's somebody coming through." And they'd say, "Well, let them go then." Then the next guys, they'd keep track of, you know, where everybody went. The next day, they would find them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you go overseas then?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Oh, golly.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: '44 maybe?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah, on the --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you spend any time in England before you went over?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We were at Bournemouth. Yeah, we went -- that was our -- well, we went to Glasgow first, in Scotland, and then went down to Bournemouth, which was -- at that time was kind of a spa. It was one of the -- well, now it's -- it's a big place where everybody kind of like -- well, a big area where everybody goes to rest and have their vacation areas. But when we were there, they had -- they -- they didn't confiscate the houses, but they would -- evidently in England, they -- I'm sure we paid for it, but we would take over all their homes, and we would stay in all these houses and just be there and finish our training there before the overseas. And that was when everybody had the -- oh, you just had to get over there. You know, I mean, you wanted to get over there before it was over and, you know, this business of wanting to do something. Until it happened, and then you wished why -- why this anxiety to get your -- get yourself blown away, which was -- and so we finally did go over. And when we got over, our group went over on LSTs, which are for tanks and for big mobile units, and we -- which was -- I got -- was beginning to get seasick on that. We were all down below, so I said, "I think I'll go up on the -- sit in my vehicle up on the deck." I went up there, and then I happened to be where I could see the point of the deck, and it was going up and down. It was awful. I thought, this is no place for me to be, up here. So we -- we finally got over there, and we landed, and it was -- and it was -- one of the old doors come down, and it wasn't -- thank goodness, it wasn't like the landing that some of these guys had, you know, where they never made it to the -- to the beach. I mean -- and that's what seems so bad, when you -- it's like chess. Well, you got so many men here. Well, we're going to lose this many no matter what, I mean, so -- and you think, am I one of those guys who they are expecting not to come back? You know, but you -- you had that. And we didn't have -- have to go through that. But you had snipers all the time, and that was -- that's -- that's the bad part.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when do you think it was that you got to France, approximately?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Must have been in --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Fall maybe?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: August -- yeah. Well, August. August or September.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you --

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: It must have been at least six weeks after --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: After D-Day?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: After D-Day. And it was -- those -- let's see. The -- there was a lot of pockets that weren't cleared out, I mean, you didn't have direct stuff right at that time, but you -- the armies were beginning, you know, to all go inwards, and everything happened from October till December. And then in December, they had the big wazoo.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day in combat, when you realized they were shooting at you?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Oh, yes. I -- yeah. I'm trying to think. Jesus, that takes a long time. That's so far -- you know, at the time I remember worse was when -- was during the Bulge, when I -- when we had to go through the town. I mean, it was after -- it was on the -- that was on the 16th. We had -- we had pulled back after we were shelled all day, and I was mortar corporal. I had -- they had me stay out there and keep -- you know, I could see from my point where -- over the hill down there is where they all were coming up, and that -- my job was to keep them there, you know, with the mortar, you know, you could control it, and so that's where I did most of my shooting. But then things were flying all around you at that -- I mean, those are the times you remember, I mean, most on this type of thing. But I wasn't hit at that time for anything. But it's -- so then we pulled back, and then we were surrounded. And then the -- the Germans came down to a crossroad with a white flag. And our lieutenant, he was named Elmo Johnson. He went down there to see them. And they said we're surrounded, did they want to -- did we want to give up or -- or lose people, you know, and fight. And he said, well, we weren't going to surrender, and he turned around and walked back up. And I thought, that makes good movie material, but a lot of times -- when it's your neck on the line, I'm not so sure about that. So we had a big meeting together and -- well, there was one road through the Town of Schonberg, which was the one avenue they might get out. So they said they're going to send a -- one squad down there to go through it, and that -- we had about 11 guys who were going to take an armored car and the rest Jeeps to go through it. And I thought, well, it will be the third squad. It won't be mine. And so I thought -- and so I settled back, and all of a sudden, it's going to be the third -- it's going to be mine, and so we did. I mean, that -- and I was in the last Jeep. Everybody else started going down this little hill. Then you could see it, you know, a little town. And the houses came right up from the streets. The street was there. It was just wide enough for, say, two vehicles. You know how they were in the little -- the little towns like that? And I had -- you could see the gun fire out there, and you could see the other Jeeps had got hit. They were off on the side, and you knew you had to go through it. There was no other way of -- there's no getting back. So you -- and so I was on the hood. I had the driver, and I put the windshield down. And I had a submachine gun on the hood, and we had a 30-caliber gun mount. And I told the guy, I said, "Just before we go through this town," I said, "you shoot up one side. I'll shoot up the other and see if we could keep the guns" -- because they would kind of -- you'd see all these windows, and all of a sudden, you'd see -- all the guns would poke out, and you'd see -- well, so you knew where they were. They were all, you know, waiting. And my big thrill of the day was, was I going to get shot? And I -- knowing you're going to have to go through it. It's just like you were in a shooting gallery. And so we started down there. And you could hear it and see it. And then a bullet hit in the back of my helmet. This is when -- a real miracle. And it crawled up between the helmet liner and the helmet, you know, your steel helmet, and blew a hole out the front. I had a headache, but I thought, my gosh, they have a bead on me. You know, I mean, they -- I mean, you really were hit then, and -- but you weren't shot, I mean. So I thought, well -- so you kept going through, and then it hit -- they hit my foot, because it was sticking out. And I -- it went in the side and broke over the -- your arch, blew off the bottom of your foot. And so you knew then what it was like. And then I thought, well, we were pretty much through the town and -- but you kept -- it was just -- just like bees all around you, you know, because it was whirling. And so we got almost through the town, and you thought well, you -- doggone it, you almost made it, and the guy blew up the back of our vehicle. I mean, it was -- they had something like -- it wasn't their -- it was their type of what a bazooka would be for ours, and the guy was standing back there, and he shot and it hit the undercarriage, threw us all into the ditch, and we were -- that was a surprise. Because there was a couple of other guys down there, and I didn't know who they were. They weren't from our outfit, but they had arm wounds. And so I asked them, I said, "Are you guys okay?" No, they weren't okay. You know, so I said, "Well, jeez, where is your sulfa?" You know, that was a big thing in those days, was the sulfa, I guess. So I wrapped up -- poured it on them and wrapped their arms up, and then I took care of mine and wrapped my foot and I just -- the sole was gone off it. I just wrapped everything around it, you know, kept the top, the boot on. And then I saw American six by six come by, and I said, "Well, at least, by God, somebody's coming up to help you." Because you could see the markings on there. And out of the back, it stopped, and out came all these young SS kids. They kept going, and I thought, my gosh. The driver got out and got on the -- and got on the fender and was going to shoot all of us that were in the ditch. And I thought, man, this is something. And so this Kaplan, he was a Jewish boy. He was a corporal. He stood up. He had a submachine gun, and he shot from the hip and hit him and killed the driver. And I thought, wow, this is -- this is going to antagonize somebody, because you don't -- because they -- you were really over -- overmanned in gun power and anything that you had. And they just went over and covered him up. And I thought, well, maybe they didn't like the driver too much. I don't know. Because they didn't -- they didn't make too much out of it. But then they come over to the rest of us and got everybody going, and they wanted everybody to get up and get going. So they told the one, two guys next to me to get up. First the first one to get up, and he said he couldn't. I mean, they were scared. We were all scared, you know. But he couldn't, and they shot him. And I thought, holy crap. And then they did that to the next guy, and he couldn't get up either. And they just had arm wounds. And I thought, holy cow, get up. And he put the thing to my head and told me to rausch mit and I said, "Right." And I mean, you have time to think, by the time -- because I thought to myself, what if they had asked me first and, you know, I had a leg wound, and I thought, well, I -- I knew the other two guys could get up. But I got up, and I hopped. And some of the guys -- then they started taking our guys down the street because it started to clear and their air corps ____, and they started strafing the road, and then we were going back. And I thought, my gosh, and so I started to hop. And then a couple of guys came that must have -- where they came from were down -- they were artillery men, and they came, and they let me, you know, helped you, helped you hop, or they -- you can kind of lean on them and you could kind of -- you could move, and then so we started going back down towards the -- the little town that we just passed through. And this -- then that's when we saw this Sergeant Bankston. He was out -- and when we went through the town, I saw him. I saw him raise his head up like this, so you know he was wounded, but he was -- you know, how -- but when we were going back, you could tell he was -- he was mortally wounded. I mean, he couldn't go anyplace. So Kaplan, he was -- he knew him real well. So he said, "I'm going to go see what I can do for him." And we had a couple of guards there, and they said, "You go out there, I'm going to shoot you." And he -- oh, they didn't care. So he just went -- they didn't shoot him. Why, I -- they seemed to take compassion on him, I guess. And so he went out and, you know, Wade told him, Kappy, what to tell his wife and everything, so he said he would. And then later, when he did get back, he did call his wife and tell her. So we went to the -- after that, we went back down on the -- we all stopped, thank goodness, for a while. And then we went back down to -- as we got into the town, it got more extreme, the strafing, and there was a barn right there, so I kind of -- I said, "Guys, I'm going to hop into that place in there." And so I hopped over in there. There were all these little townspeople in there, and they were mad as ticks, you know. They didn't want to be bombed, and we were the cause. And they all had their pitchforks and stuff. And I thought, oh, where am I now? And so we were -- we were in there for a while. And pretty soon everything cooled off long enough, they rounded everybody up again. And they took all the Americans and put them over in one spot, and then they took me over, and they were going to take me into a little house that was right next -- there were a lot of burned-out buildings on the other side, but this one side. And there was a doorway, and I -- there was -- Germans were in there and this one American solder. And I looked in there and it was Sam Massarsky, and he's from our troop. And I had said, "How the heck did Sam get in there?" He waved to me, and I waved back. And there was a gun lying right on the table, I mean, a gun that was unattended, you might say. And all of a sudden, I saw him, you know, reach for it. And the guard turned me around and got me like -- and I heard two shots. So I don't know. I heard later that he was killed, but I don't know whether it was from that -- I mean, I -- I couldn't say I saw him dead. But from what he was doing, he was reaching for a gun and -- and it was filled -- the rest of that house had all Germans in it. And why I was going to be going up in there and then they turned me away, I don't know. Those are one of the, you know, say mystery things that happens and you wonder why. And so that night, they took me into this little kind of like a cowshed, and it was getting -- it was dark by then, and I couldn't see anybody, so I went in there and laid down. It was nothing you could do. And then I heard these voices, and I thought, oh, my gosh. What is it? And I thought, well, it's Americans. So I don't know what I said, something like "Hey" or something, you know. You don't know. And then you could tell it was German talk came back. And I thought, oh, my, this is -- what am I in now? Because I know I wasn't with Americans then. And this one, he had been wounded. I don't know where or how, but all his jaw was off. I mean, he had -- and he had had this little cup he was drinking, and he offered me a cup of whatever it was. I assume it must have been tea or hot water or something. And I just felt well, there must be kind of compassion of some kind among, you know, guys that are wounded, no matter what side you're on. And so that was -- that was it on that for that night. Then the next day, they piled us all in this little lorry. It was horse-drawn with two guards. And we went back -- I didn't know where we were going, but you saw all kinds of debris, and the towns and everything that were destroyed and all the stuff. And you saw tanks that had -- you know, they had their big Tiger tanks. They had the big spikes, and they would put these trees on them, you know, and then they tie them so they look like -- for camouflage, you know. But they -- and you'd see -- all of a sudden, they'd start moving, and you could tell this was a big push. And you could see the cycle troops, all the guys on bicycles riding, you know, and how they did that in the snow and all this junk, I don't know. But they were all pumping along there, going away. And it was kind -- it was -- it was interesting to see what was happening when you were, let's say, almost a noncombatant. It's kind of like you're watching a movie-type thing, when you're -- you're in somebody else's hand. The game is over as far as -- you know, I mean, the only thing is you want to get yourself tagged. I wanted to get -- to become a prisoner then. Because, you know, our -- all our talk and everything that we get, you know, on when you're a prisoner is escape, you know. And there's no reason to ever be caught, you know, for -- they say this. And Patton gives quite a little talk on that. "Don't get caught." And -- but the idea that if you -- if you can't, I mean, if you have no weapons, where are you going to go? Just -- you aren't going to run away on something and get shot just for what. And my idea was, I didn't want to be like this Malmedy thing, where they had these men in these trucks and let them out for a little leg rest or whatever and then they shot them all. And I -- why they wanted me, I don't know. I was the only American there, and I was -- and I was really a detriment to them. I couldn't walk. Well, I could hop, but then we were -- but I wasn't any good as far as a prisoner. Why would -- why would they keep you? And I don't know why, but that was -- that's -- they did. And then so we spent days -- well, let's see. From the 17th and I think until about the 20th. No, it must have been a little longer than that. It must have been -- how many days would that be? I'm trying to --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So were you separated then from the other prisoners? Is that what you're saying?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: From the American prisoners, yes. I wasn't with -- just --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that right away that you think that happened?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. And that's what bothered me. Because, you know, I mean, it's enough -- you're under enough stress, I mean, being caught. I mean, it's like being in a ball game and it's the third strike and oh, okay, you're out. But this way it's -- you know, in the Army, you're -- you're caught, and what happens? I mean, you know, when you're 21, it's -- it's a whole different ball game right then.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And you told me you went back with the German wounded then. Right?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah. Well, they put me with the German wounded, I mean, on the lorry. And that first night, when I was in the little shed, that was with Germans.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: So, I mean, see, the other Americans there weren't -- that -- with -- during that period when we went through the town weren't wounded. None of them. I was the only one that was wounded. There were two guys who -- wherever they came from or from what outfit, I -- you know, at a time like that, you don't ask. I mean, things are happening so fast, you just take care of business and that's it. And so -- and then they didn't survive. And, you know, so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And you told me you had a hand grenade in your pocket?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah, a hand grenade and a mortar sight. But you had these deep pockets, you know, and you don't really notice it until all of a sudden, you think, holy cow, what have I got. You know, because when we were going through this town, you thought, well, you carry as much different stuff as you could, you know, while you were going through. But I had forgotten about it, and -- and so you had that till I got to the -- well, once we got to a church on this going back to the railroad cars, which is -- must have been around the 21st or one of those. Because we were on the road about five or six days in this lorry, and you just stop at night, and they'd have bombed-out buildings, and you had -- the guards would be there, and it was -- it was just -- and you never -- I never thought about anything else because you never really felt it, you know, because it was way down in -- and, you know, you were hopping, and you weren't doing any -- anything else. And so you just -- you were just existing until you got to this -- I don't know the name of the town, but it had a great big cathedral there, and they'd made it into a German hospital for their -- for the Germans. And we -- as we came close to it, there was another air raid. And I thought, oh -- and that was when things really started to clear up for, you know, the Bulge part, you know. They -- it cleared up enough where the Army or the Air Corps could get out and do more good, and they started. And so I got out of that lorry, and I ran -- hopped into that church and -- I'm telling you. And then I saw -- there I saw some Americans. They were kind of huddled around. And I said, "Oh, jeez. There's somebody I can say something to." And then they -- the bombing became more intense. So we all went down in this basement they had down below the first floor, and we stayed there, and then the Germans would -- piled right after us. And pretty soon, they -- when it was over, they would round us up again and took us out to the train. There was -- it must have been a -- the Germans must have had calvary or something that they used to carry on these little tiny Turnerville Train things, and -- and they were all full of horse manure and straw, and they tried to -- threw the straw over all that, you know, and tried to make it -- but a stinky old place. But they loaded us on there and got all the guards in there, and they opened both doors, and that's how we rode into -- into Stalag 11b Christmas Eve. And it was snowing that night, and I thought, this is -- this is a nice place to be on a night like this, Christmas. And we stood out there for three hours. It was cold. Oh, my gosh. You had these long lines of guys, you know, getting in there. And when they get there, they just -- your name, rank, and serial number. And they said, Okay. We're going to put -- put you guys just -- tomorrow we'll interrogate everybody, but put them in their little -- someplace to -- beds or, you know, just something, you know. They had to get you out of the weather. And they were really ramshackle little -- little huts, almost. So we went in there with a couple of the other guys, and they had one little -- like in a movie, a little hanging lightbulb in the center and it was dark. And I thought, man, this is something else. And I thought, my God, that's -- you know the walls had, you know, little cracks, you know, because they were all lapped wood. And I said, "You've got to get rid of this stuff on you, because tomorrow you're going to really be scrutinized real good." And so I -- I saw this bunk over in the corner. They were all little -- not -- they weren't -- they were metal, you know, little crazy little things. And I said, "Oh, my God, look. Right in this corner, an awful big rat hole. It's big enough for this little old -- little hand grenade I got and mortar sight." So I chucked them down there. And I thought, I hope nobody comes by here later and pulls that pin, or we're going to have a real -- have a real time, because it's live. So I got rid of that. And the next day, on Christmas, they took us in in groups of about five or ten, you know, and they -- then the officer would say, "Okay. All the 106th move over there. Those in the 212 over there." And all these guys would fall out -- you know, they -- you know, you're conditioned to where if somebody say go here and go over there. And there's three of us then in the middle. And they said, "Where are you from?" And so we said, "All we have to give is our name, rank, and serial number." And they were getting testy over that. But we said, "Hey, that's it." And I thought, Bob, you've come this far, are you going to -- are we going to lose it here on the final -- but I just figured that was -- that's what we had been told to say, and they said that was what -- all you had -- did have to say. And you probably -- they probably knew where you were from anyhow, you know, because you had patches on and stuff, but I -- so that's all the three of us said, so they said, "Okay. You guys go over there." So then they -- they assessed what was wrong with your wounds and where you should go. Should you go down to the lager, which is where the guys that weren't wounded could be, or would you be up in the -- in the -- up on a hill -- excuse me -- where the housing was for -- they called it the hospital part. It was -- it was the same as the things down there, except you didn't have to go out and stand revelry in the morning. I think that was the only different part of the whole dumb thing, but -- so that's where I went. I got in there. And it was different. You met different guys, and they -- these rooms were -- they had wooden beds or bunks, you know. They had about six slats, and they brought some ticks in there, and you'd fill them with straw and put on there. But you didn't have any blankets or anything. They didn't have things of that nature.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you say you lost a week that you can't remember then from that time?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: No, no. The time I lost was when -- between --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The capture and --

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: -- between when we went -- once I was on that lorry to getting on the --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Train?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: -- the train. And that's where -- it was just -- pardon -- on nights -- pardon me -- it was just an all-day thing. And, you know, I don't think they went that far because -- but, you know, because with a horse-drawn thing they had to stop it and everybody would get out, and then you'd stop at these bombed-out little places, little dinky little towns, and they'd give you something to eat. And I thought it was butter, but it was lard. I thought, my God, this is lard, you know, because it had that bacony kind of -- but they were just little squares, and that's -- that's all you had. And so we -- that was the part where I really -- well, you -- you're in a mindset of not knowing, I mean, what's going -- you're really concerned about what's somebody going to -- at home going to -- how will they -- when will they know. So, you know, you have this feeling of worry from, you know, how everybody does and how they're going to feel. Because you know, they get stuff over the radio, well, they captured somebody or the Bulge has started and all this, and they -- no one really knows, so I -- that was a part where I really couldn't remember. And I thought, how did I ever get there? Then after we talked -- talked about that, oh, jeez, you know, it -- it -- like a little light comes up on. Yeah, that's how that happened, so...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So just in shock or whatever --

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Well, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- or whatever --

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah. And thing is, you're hurting, and the biggest thing is you're trying to take care of -- I didn't have any more sulfa or anything. I had used it all up. So the only thing I could do is just exist until we got into the prison camp. And then when we did finally get in the -- a room for, you know, people that were -- had wounds and stuff like that, they -- they had a doctor in there that was King Peter's private physician. He -- because they had a lot of Yugoslavians in there, and he volunteered his service. You could tell he wasn't hurting for anything because he was doing good, so he got -- but which is -- I guess is all right. But they were the ones that would take care of you. And they got me in my turn to come in, and they said -- looked at my foot and they, hmm. It had about -- a hole about the size of a dime where the entrance and the bottom was all blown off. So they took a wire and put it in the side and went out -- went out the bottom. If you don't think there was a little anxiety then? Because I tried to tell them then it was perforated. But, you know, how are you going to say -- I went like this and out, you know, made motions on -- that they wanted to make sure there was nothing in there, I guess. I don't know. But they had two Germans standing there, standing like this, watching. And I just went -- I said, "Well, by golly, you aren't going to get any yell out of me." But, man, I had to stuff it up. When you're young, you can do -- I couldn't do that anymore. But they really did a job, and then -- so they wrapped it with just -- they didn't have any medicines. They just wrapped it in paper. And they had some water, and they said sterile water. The guys with his hands, he'd wipe it off. Like that's sterile water on my foot, you know. They had the paper that kind of stretched. Oh, I don't know. And they'd wrap that up and that kept festering up. And finally, on my birthday, they said they were going to take it off. And I said, "No, no. No takey -- no takey off." And I don't know -- but -- and they didn't. They said, well, we'll try putting a cast on it with a hole around, you know, where the entrance -- bullet hole went in because that was just -- that was just getting awful. So they did. And then that really -- oh that came out like a rotten tomato. It just puffed up out of there. And I thought, oh, I hope they didn't want to put me into the cast room. END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah, uh-huh. Because it really smelled. They kept that door closed, and it just smelled. Because their method of healing in there was putting maggots on there, you know, and it does do the job. It eats all the dead flesh, but it smelled terrible. And I thought, I don't want to get put in there, you know, because I was in this other room. And they -- finally, I told them, I said, "Take this thing off. It's going to -- it looks like" -- well, you know how things, how they -- well, you don't know, but they keep festering up. And it looked like a rotten tomato, just -- you know how they looked -- how it blows out of the hole that they had there for them. So they took it off, just wrapped it, and that was the way it was until I got to the -- England. It gradually -- I think it must have started -- but all the bones were solidified in there, you know, on the -- in your foot. But the opening -- or kind of -- or the bottom started to heal up now and the opening on the top, but splinters would come out every little bit, every now and then, you know, poke through, and it did a long time after I was -- you know -- well, on my foot now, it's still -- there's a little bump on that side, and it's still bruised after 60 years and -- but we got that -- that was resolved. And the only other thing we had in there was these different guys that you were with, and you find out, in these days, how they -- who real friends are and -- because we had one guy in there that was an old tanker and, you know, they'd bring your food in. You'd get a piece of bread, a little potato, and your klim tin of soup. And klim tin was milk spelled backwards. I don't know where they --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I've heard that. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Oh, you've heard it? Okay. And that was there. That was your eating facility there. And so we -- we -- and a lot of times you'd save a little of that for later, you know. You'd put a -- we had a little -- kind of like a cabinet, you know, a little homemade thing, it seemed like it was. But everybody had a place where you could keep your own stuff. And they found him once going over eating and taking some other guy's stuff. They threw him -- the guys that could, picked him up and threw him right out the window. I don't know whatever happened to him. I mean, we're on the first floor, but he was still gone. And I don't know whatever -- we never saw him again, so I don't know where -- they might have put him down with the boys downstairs or down in the walking -- walking guys. But we had this Sergeant Rosata. He was the one that was -- he was the reigning noncom in there who would take all the complaints and, you know, he would be able to settle arguments. You know, you had to have somebody do the -- do all that, you know, and so he was. And then his arm was so bad, I thought he'd never get out. But then, after a while, he -- they transferred him to someplace else. I don't know where it was. That's when I lost contact with him. But he was -- he was a nice fellow. He was a big Italian guy that knew his way around. But he was -- he was only there for a short time too. I mean -- I mean, as far as, you know, being overseas and then all of a sudden, they got taken right away which was --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you in the hospital the whole time then while you were in prison?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Uh-huh, all the time. Yeah. And we -- you could see how they treated the other prisoners, people like -- I hope that doesn't bother your thing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Too late to worry about it now.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Oh, okay. The -- like the Yugoslavians and different ethnic groups, they would feed them just almost like hogs. They had these big troughs out there. They'd throw the stuff out. You'd see these people groveling around in there, eating and taking their pans. That was awful. But you really saw who they -- because with them, evidently the Geneva Convention didn't matter too much, you know, as far as maybe they were concerned. But they tried to keep it as much with us as they could. They would -- we had two Red Cross boxes come. And the first time it came, they -- before they came, they brought us blankets and all -- all kind of stuff, and then we got our box. And we thought -- we didn't open it. We said, "We'll wait till these guys go, and then we'll eat this stuff." And then the guys left -- they wouldn't let you talk to them, to the Red Cross. They'd come in just -- and they've have to look around and, you know, they'd just wander around. But then when they left, they took everything back. We said, "Hmm, poor thinking. We should have eaten while we had that." They took the blankets and everything. So the next time they came through, we ate -- we opened things up while they were there. Because, you know, you learn after a while. But it was -- every day was just like -- just you could see your breath in there the whole time. It was -- I mean, it was cold. I mean, it was just very -- but you were young. You could tolerate things of that nature. It was -- and you just hoped you could, you know, keep it up. Because there's a time that, you know, you thought, what if we lost the war? I mean, you know, after -- it seems like eternity that you're ever, you know, in there, even though it's not -- say it's only about four and a half to five months, you know. You think it's forever if you're young. And you think, they don't even have to come get me. I mean, I'm right here. And so the -- that's a thought that, you know -- and then I -- so I had started doing a little drawing. I had little scraps of paper, and I'd just draw stuff, pictures of some of the guys, you know, just some kind of fun thing. And these British would come in, and they'd say, gee, you know, like we said before, did I want some paints and a pencil and stuff? You know, you say yes, but you think well, how -- where is this coming from? And the next day, they -- these guys brought it in. And then this British corporal Morgan, he asked if you wanted paper, and he got it. I said, "Where did you get that?" "That's morgue paper. They wrap the bodies in this." "Oh, thank you. Good." So it makes -- I mean, I had a big roll of it, you know, so I could just tear it off, you know, when you wanted to draw this. And so the drawings looked raggedy, but they're original, and that's all that I -- that you are -- that's all you care about now. I mean, at the time, it was a method of keeping -- of surviving. Really, of keeping alive. Because it's surprising these guys -- you know, anybody that draws, people are interested because they think -- well, it's something to look at outside of each other. And you're all in a sad state, you know, really, but, you know, you aren't -- nobody is having much fun. And it made kind of an interesting thing, and they all took care of watching out for you and stuff like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, had you drawn before you were captured?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Oh, I went to school for -- for art, you know. I mean, I wanted to -- that's what I wanted to get into, was art somewhere along the line, you know, in -- there's so many ways, you know, in those days. Now it's all computerized. I'm just glad I was there when I -- when it's you. I mean, the -- this is not taking away from computers and stuff like that because that's -- they're excellent. But the people nowadays, I mean, it's -- the personal element is gone. I mean, you get it first, but the thing now with art is you're making money. They want to make money so you -- okay. It's there. You do it on a computer, you can get it, "bing, bing, bing, bing." Where before it's a labor of love when you have -- just like all the Disney stuff is being done by -- by computers now, which is -- it's too bad because a lot of guys are good at that kind of stuff. And it was fun. It was fun doing things for people like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And it's kind of hard to talk about the drawings much. I hope people listening to this tape could someday see some of these drawings.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You drew scenes of camp life?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You said you drew horses at first?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Well, because that's -- well, when I was a kid I liked horses. That's why I got in horse calvary. I thought that would, you know, be -- I wasn't expecting to go to war with it, but I thought -- you know, when you go into school, you know, you had to take ROTC, and that was one of the things; that or field artillery or the infantry, so I thought that was best. I liked that because that's -- you wore the jodhpurs and boots, and I thought that's -- that's good for girl quality. Except when you'd go -- when you'd go out to the barns and work and you had this stuff on and then you'd go to class, you smelled just like the barn. You weren't -- nobody wanted to get that close you to anyhow. But it was -- but I -- go ahead.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, I was going to say that I -- just so the people are clear that are listening, you had to draw these things secretly --

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- and then keep it hidden. Right?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah. I'd keep it in the ticks. I made a little -- I even forget where we got the little cardboardy stuff. One of the guys said they'd stamp it together, so they'd -- you can get pretty much anything, I guess, if they -- some of these people. So they -- they put it together, so I -- I just would tear the sheets off the same size. But none of this was done with the idea that -- of showing it or doing anything with it later. It was just -- it was -- it was a means of biding your time and -- what's nice, if you -- if you have a -- call it a talent, I mean, where you can use it and it takes your mind off of your pains and all the other stuff. Because I spent a good share of my time with my leg up in the air. It's -- you know when it's -- you know just like when you have a hurt on your finger and when your hand's down, how it throbs on your -- any extremity, it seems like it pounds. And when you have it on your foot like that, it really would -- you know, especially when you'd hop, you would feel it a lot. And so I had -- that's why I always wanted a top bunk, so I could kind of swing up and then keep your -- my -- I could keep my foot -- you know, I could just stay there and just -- seemed like I could -- I had visualized the blood rushing down -- down my leg instead of, you know, pounding into it. Not that that makes any sense, but you had a feeling that you were helping yourself on a screwy way.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else from camp life that you remember, prison camp life?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Well, no. They played a lot of cards. I mean, I never liked -- watch -- I just watched. A lot of them wanted you to play -- a lot of them played bridge, you know. They wanted to teach you bridge. But a lot of these younger kids and I -- and then the others wanted to play -- you know, they would play poker, which is -- when they had matchsticks and little -- they would devise all kind of little things to -- to use for money. And, I mean, so it wasn't -- nobody was getting anything. It was time passing, and that was one of the things you did. And it got so cold at times, and you spent a lot of times picking lice. I mean, you wanted to make sure because they said if -- if -- what is it you get from lice, if you get a big -- oh, goodness. Not -- typhus, is it? No, not, typhus. What is it you get when you get -- they said if it started, they would -- everybody in that room would be gone, would be gone. They would exterminate everyone because they didn't want it to start, whatever it is. I -- "it" leaves -- it leaves me at this moment. I have it written down.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'm sure it's some --

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: But it's -- but at the -- and so that made you very conscious of -- you know, that's why I made a lot of drawings of that, of guys -- and you had to do it between your two thumbs and you had to crack them and then you had the residue get on, and you had to think of the guy down there, "Oh, gosh, get out of here. Don't put them on me." And then you had to go -- because they -- the lice would get into the folds of the clothes, you know, and you didn't have any -- no place to bathe or -- we had one shower. On my birthday, they said, "Okay. Everybody's going into the showers." And I thought, oh, my, in the showers that -- because you knew about, you know, in these other prison camps where the shower was the place for getting rid of people. And they had one of these big stacks and all this stuff. And oh, my. How is this going to work? But it was just a shower, so that was the one time they got clean -- I mean, your clothes weren't any cleaner, but you got a chance to get some of the grime off of you, I guess, and it was -- but that was on my birthday. I remember that. But it was --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Your parents were notified that you were missing in action shortly after you were captured?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: No, no. They -- oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were missing?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: That I was missing, yeah. Yeah, and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And can you tell how long it took for them to figure out you were a prisoner?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. They didn't know until I was almost released. And they gave us these little -- as you saw, the little postcards. And you'd give it to these guys, and they'd smile their sweet smiles, you know, and take them. Then you'd see them put them all in the bag. Then you see them out with the bag burning, where they had these little pot holes out there, and they'd throw them all in there. And you'd think, you know, nobody is going to know where you are. And the only way, if you wanted to send anything, is to make sure -- was to say everything was good. I mean, make sure, because they read them all, you know, they made sure. If you said anything detrimental, it wouldn't go through. So the ones that I did send, I just said everything was fine. You're getting good care, you know. What else are you going to say? Well, it makes them feel good at home anyhow, and so it wasn't -- it wasn't necessarily -- if you wanted it to get through, that's what you did --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So it was about four months before your parents got official notification --

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- that you were a POW?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Uh-huh. Then I went --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And that was almost the end of war?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah. Then I went to England then. And -- oh, that other thing, when we were -- just we -- you could tell when the camp was about to be taken by the Allies. And the Germans -- or the Russians were coming from one end and the English from another, and we were coming from another angle. We wanted -- everyone was, which -- which Army was going to set us free, you know, and -- well, you know, and the French Underground would come in with their little radios each day and tell you the news. One day they were here, the next day the Armies were there. You know, I mean, I had little camp newspapers that they had, you know, that would tell stuff like that and -- but they -- no one really knew. So when it came down to the last week, you could hear artillery so you knew somebody was out close. So they would put an American, a British and a -- and I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Perhaps French at that point?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah, probably, probably a French, yeah, on the guard post. And they took all the young Germans off the post and put an old guy on there with them, and so whoever came through, they could talk, you know, with the -- or say, "Don't shoot the guard" or "Shoot him." But on that day, when they came through, they -- we went outside. It was in the middle of the morning, and you could see this little old German cart was racing down the street just pellmell, and this British tank was right after it, shooting him. They weren't -- they were just trying to see how fast he'd go. They didn't care, you know, if they hit him. But you could tell that little old man that was in it, you know, just going like crazy and this big tank rolling right after, you know, the gun, "pow, pow," you know, just powing right after him. And all of a sudden, it turned right into the camp and rolled down that fence and the really hoopla came then. And it was the British. The British were the one. And the -- so there was a lot that went on during that day. And Montgomery came into our room because we had a -- one of the guys that was in there was a British fellow that jumped at Arnhem, and he was kind of like the atrocity case of -- he was just skin and bones. I mean, if you wanted to study how the bones was on a living person, I mean, that's what -- he just lay there. And he was -- and Montgomery came in the room. I made a drawing of that. And he had his drum sergeant, which must have been three heads or shoulders higher than him. Montgomery is just a little guy, he had a little bit of a mustache and just a real cute little fellow. But they were very -- got their man out of there, talked for a little bit, turned around and left. But it was -- but it was interesting to see somebody like that in your room.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did he talk to you at all?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: No, not at -- not personally, but he just talked to the guys, how they were -- they were free now, but we were -- well, we were free. We didn't have to go anyplace. But we were there about three weeks eating British oatmeal. At least that was -- maybe that's all we could really tolerate. I don't know. But we had that. And then they asked any of us that wanted to, did we want to stay and be guards, you know, be guards at the camp, you know, for duty of any kind. And some of the guys -- then they had to screen you if you did because they didn't want guys trying to get back at somebody, you know, and -- no, I want to get out of here, so they didn't. So we stayed there for almost -- it seemed like forever -- three weeks or so. And then we -- they took us to a landing strip, and we were there for about another week, lying on a little cot in there, and then we got out. And then the plane came for us, I mean, it was getting near the time when they could be -- but we didn't know it then, the war could end. But then they took us to England. I was one of the first ones put on the plane. Did I -- they said, "You want to have" -- because we were all on cots, you know, and those planes are all empty, you know, and then they had things for -- "Do you want to have a window where you can see the Channel?" I says, "No. Put me right up there in the top. I'm going to go to sleep." That's the first time I slept for ages, since I found -- I didn't have to worry about anybody else or I didn't think I did, you know. And they -- that's the way I went over there. The other guys would stand in the window and looked. I said, "I could care less. I just -- get me -- get me someplace safe." So then I went to a hospital, a Quonset hut place. And I was there for quite a while, and they -- well, they put me in a private room first because they didn't want us to -- if we had anything, to give it to any of the guys in the hospital there. So I -- but they fed you. My gosh, I began to balloon out because they had a little place where you could go and eat if you wanted to. I had crutches then so I could, you know, get around. I didn't have to hop. And then they put me into the regular hospital. That was this little Quonset just lined with beds on both sides and must have had about 30 or 40 guys at one place. And you'd see -- at one end you'd see these guys throwing what looked like a ball, and it was a guy. He had no arms or legs. He had all -- and they were throwing him, you know -- I mean, they were all good-natured. "But, hey, let's throw Charlie around." And, you know, it's kind of sad. I mean, as long as they're all together like that, it's all right. I mean, but, you know, someday, he's going to have to go home and -- like that, and he won't have the camaraderie of somebody to kind of shield you and know what you've gone through and stuff like that. And then there was a fellow in the bed right next to me who was all covered up except for his head. And I talked to him and, you know, you got to be friendly. But he always wanted something. And this was when I first met him. He needed the nurses all the time. All the time, every second he seemed to need something. Finally, I said, "What the heck is wrong with you?" I don't even remember his name anymore. And he said, "I was a tail gunner. I was shot out of a plane, and I went straight down into a new-mowed field or a new-plowed field, and I went down right into it up to my neck." He said, "I think I broke every bone" in his body. He said the Germans were so surprised and astounded that he was still alive, they dug him out and took him to a hospital, and they had -- took him to their hospital, and then they -- they sent him to an American hospital, they were so, you know, amazed and -- that somebody could go through that, you know. I mean, he had every -- every bone, everything was all broke. And I -- so I had a different feeling about him then. If he wanted something, I would help him, you know, usually and -- because it seemed like he would just kind of, you know -- nobody -- nobody in there was really healthy, you know. Everybody had something. But I thought he was just a complainer, you know, and he wasn't. He really was somebody. So you got to know him, and he was -- he said he had a cattle ranch. He said, "You know, some day I'll get back out there and do that." And I thought, well, maybe -- maybe you will, and maybe you won't. I -- but, you know, all of a sudden, he's shipped out and, you know, they get -- they go home, and they go for different places or they -- different hospitals. And then I was getting set to go home.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Before we get to that, did -- his parachute didn't open?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He actually --

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: He just -- just went right --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- fell and hit into the soft --

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: -- right in this --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- soft field.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: -- soft -- it was a new-plowed field.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: They said they couldn't believe that that could happen. Well, I -- and jeez, because they really made a lot out of it. I mean -- I mean, once you knew what it was, then you heard the other attendants that were at the hospital there, they said, oh, jeez -- and it was -- you know, at the time like that, you don't take down names. You don't make notes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Because it's just like at the hospital, you know, if you have somebody next to you, you say hi and you know them for that time. But then after a few years or whatever, you forget. But you remember incidents like that, where these guys --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure. Of course.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: So -- just -- it was something else to see him like that. And he -- but he was good -- he really was good-natured for having such distress.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So then you came home?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah. Well -- oh, and before I came home, I got yellow jaundice. They didn't know what it was. Oh, I -- my eyes turned yellow. I looked just like a real cartoon Chinaman. And then I was on crutches, so I went into the bathroom to the urinal, and I would urinate, and it was just like red, like ketchup. It was real thick, and it was real red, and I was like, "Holy cripes, what have I got?" So they put me in isolation because they thought maybe it was yellow fever, you know, you know, whatever. Because they didn't -- because I was all set to be flown home because, you know, POWs they'd -- they'd fly you home. And they -- this -- when they put me in isolation until they found out, they said, "Well, you got a heck of a case of" -- what is it with your liver you get?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was it?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: We know --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Hepatitis?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Hepatitis, yeah. And that was -- that was -- with the jaundiced part, that's what made me jaundiced, I guess, was the hepatitis. And so I finally got over that, and then they said, "Oh, you have to go back -- you have to go back on a hospital ship," and so that took quite a while to go. So they went up to Scotland again and got on a little old -- one of those little old ships, hospital ships, and went home. And I -- out in the middle of the ocean, the boiler blew on that, and so they were floating for a while. And then that was -- finally, we got home. But by that time, I could -- I could, you know, use the cane -- or not the cane. They didn't give me a cane when I got on shore, they said, because when I got -- oh, they didn't want to do anything in England for my foot because all the bones were solidified. They said, "If we do anything here, you'll have to stay here for a while for rehabilitation. Would you rather go home and have them do it there?" And so I opted for home, naturally. I said, "I'm going this far, let's go." So that's why I didn't have anything done there. But they were apprised of it. But they had stopped the infection part, but then it was -- they would have had to open everything up and start over again and, you know, get things right, I guess, or whatever. And so when I got to Percy Jones, I went -- because that was the orthopaedic place, they said, "Your -- these things are all solidified." They said, "You can walk." And they said, "You will have pain sometimes and some of the -- you'll get splinters coming out." But they said, "It will -- we -- we can either do this or you can get a 10 percent, you know, pension like that and let it go." So I said, "I'm -- I'm for getting out so I can go home." So that's --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you finally got home?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: It was great because just after I got home, by the time I got home, the war had ended in -- in --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In the Pacific?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: In the Pacific. And so Ed's outfit -- you know, when he was with the calvary, they were going to have to go over to Japan, you know, at the time. When the war ended here, he was going over there. But it ended, so he was going to be mustered out. So when I got home, about a week after I got home, then he got home -- or he -- he got home. We got a chance to be together, and then Jeanette came down with our folks, so a big happy reunion and then start back to school.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Back to school?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: And get married and all that stuff.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Very good.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Yeah. So it's -- but it's -- there's times when you feel -- on bed, whether you feel -- your foot bothers you. And there's times when you get pain and stuff, but that's -- it's not near -- I learned in the -- in the -- in the camp to prevent -- well, I couldn't prevent pain, but I could almost put myself into a feeling that pain is like a feeling. There are good feelings and bad feelings, and I'd keep telling myself, "This is a good feeling," I mean, and you could -- you could almost get yourself so you could go through by -- the pain, you know, which would be the throbbing and the -- keep going. I mean, you know, when you're by yourself, you have to do something because you don't have anybody. Because everybody else is in a boat themselves of being -- having something unpleasant. And this was your cross that you had, and so that's -- I got so I could really -- I could -- I had a high -- I got so I could get a high tolerance for pain, which didn't do me any good later in life when I would get pancreatitis because I would wait until I was almost out because I could say this is not -- because that's when it would go through your front right into your back. But I got so I could do that. I don't think I could do it anymore.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, wonderful.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Pardon me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: I think that's probably --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's very interesting, fascinating. I always -- I've done more than 200 of these interviews. I always hear things I've never heard before.

sp.speaker: Robert S. Storms
sp.p: Oh, I imagine -- I imagine you would. There's no two alike anyplace.
